cor-mix-icc-interval.title: Exact interval for the variance ratio
cor-mix-icc-interval.title_html: Exact interval for the variance ratio
cor-mix-icc-interval.html:
In the balanced normal one-way random effects model, let F=MSB/MSE and let Fq denote the q quantile of F(g−1,n−g). Then [1m(FF1−α/2−1),  1m(FFα/2−1)]{#eq-mix-gamma-interval}

is an exact 1−α confidence interval for γ=σa2/σ2, and applying the increasing map γ↦γ/(1+γ) to its endpoints gives an exact 1−α interval for the intraclass correlation ρ. Endpoints below zero are replaced by zero.

def-mix-model.title: Linear mixed model
def-mix-model.html:
Let X be a known n×p matrix and Z a known n×q matrix. The linear mixed model is 𝛃𝛆Y=Xβ+Zu+ε,{#eq-mix-model}

where 𝛃β∈Rp is a vector of unknown constants, the fixed effects; u is a q×1 random vector, the random effects, with E(u)=0 and Cov(u)=G; 𝛆ε is an n×1 random vector with 𝛆E(ε)=0 and 𝛆Cov(ε)=R; and 𝛆Cov(u,ε)=0. The matrices G and R are nonnegative definite and are known functions 𝛉G(θ), 𝛉R(θ) of an unknown parameter 𝛉θ, the variance components. The normal linear mixed model adds u∼Nq(0,G) independent of 𝛆ε∼Nn(0,R).

def-mix-oneway.title: One-way random effects model
def-mix-oneway.html: Let g≥2 groups contain nk≥1 observations each, with n=∑knk. The one-way random effects model is Ykj=μ+ak+εkj,k=1,…,g,  j=1,…,nk, where μ is an unknown constant, the group effects a1,…,ag are uncorrelated with mean 0 and variance σa2≥0, the errors εkj are uncorrelated with mean 0 and variance σ2>0, and the two sets are uncorrelated with each other. In matrix form, with Z the n×g matrix of group indicators, 𝛆Y=μ1+Za+ε. The normal one-way random effects model adds a∼Ng(0,σa2I) independent of 𝛆ε∼Nn(0,σ2I). The layout is balanced if n1=⋯=ng=m. The pair (σa2,σ2) are the variance components.

def-mix-predictor.title: Mixed functions and linear predictors
def-mix-predictor.html: In @def-mix-model, a mixed function is a random variable 𝛌𝛃τ=λ⊤β+c⊤u with known 𝛌λ∈Rp and c∈Rq. A linear predictor of τ is a statistic t=a⊤Y+b with known a and b; it is unbiased if E(t)=E(τ) for every 𝛃β∈Rp. The best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) of τ is the unbiased linear predictor minimizing the prediction mean squared error E(t−τ)2.

def-mix-reml.title: Error contrasts and restricted maximum likelihood
def-mix-reml.title_html: Error contrasts and restricted maximum likelihood
def-mix-reml.html:
Let r=rank(X). An error contrast is a random variable k⊤Y with X⊤k=0; its distribution does not involve 𝛃β. A maximal set of error contrasts is K⊤Y for an n×(n−r) matrix K of full column rank with C(K)=C(X)⊥. The restricted (or residual) log-likelihood is the log-likelihood of K⊤Y, 𝛉ℓR(θ)=−12{(n−r)log⁡2π+log⁡det(K⊤VK)+y⊤K(K⊤VK)−1K⊤y},{#eq-mix-reml-loglik}

and the REML estimate of 𝛉θ maximizes it over the parameter space.

exm-mix-boundary-size.title: What the calibration costs
exm-mix-boundary-size.html: Take g=6 groups of m=4. Exactly 0.554 of the null distribution of L sits at zero, and a simulation of 200000 data sets puts 0.554 there. Referring L to the chi-bar-squared mixture, whose 5 per cent point is the 90 per cent point 2.706 of χ2(1), gives an actual size of 0.0411: slightly conservative. Referring it to χ2(1), with critical value 3.841, gives 0.0204, badly conservative — the test throws away about half its power. With g=40 groups the mixture is nearly exact, at 0.0462. Figure 32.5.3 compares the three tail functions.

exm-mix-cluster-coverage.title: Eight clusters
exm-mix-cluster-coverage.html:
Simulate the trial with g=8 clusters of m=5, an intraclass correlation of 0.2, and no treatment effect. Over 200000 trials, the nominal 95% normal Wald interval covers 0.901 of the time, while the t(g−2) interval covers 0.949. Figure 32.5.1 traces the coverage against the number of clusters: 0.812 with four clusters, still 0.943 with forty. The normal interval’s coverage is exactly 2Ft(g−2)(1.96)−1, which is why it approaches but never reaches 0.95.

The coverage study is the null one; take now a single data set simulated from the same design but with a true effect of 0.8. On it the estimated effect is 1.154 with standard error 0.479. The normal interval is 1.154±0.940, which excludes zero; the exact interval is 1.154±1.173, which does not. The whole difference between “significant” and “not” is the reference distribution.

exm-mix-gibbs.title: The proficiency study, four ways
exm-mix-gibbs.html:
Run the sampler for 40000 draws on the data of @exm-mix-proficiency. Under the IG(0.001,0.001) prior the posterior median of σa2 is 0.0356; under the half-Cauchy prior with A=1 it is 0.0438. The REML estimate 0.0386 sits between them. The two priors therefore disagree by about a fifth of the estimate, with twelve laboratories — which is already a reason to report the prior.

The posterior means of the twelve effects track the BLUPs closely: their correlation exceeds 0.99 and the largest in absolute value is 0.294 against the BLUP’s 0.321, slightly more shrunk — not because the posterior sits below the REML estimate, since its mean 0.0431 is above it, but because the shrinkage factor B=mσa2/(σ2+mσa2) is concave in σa2: averaging B over a posterior with mass near zero weights the data less than σ^a2 does. Their posterior standard deviations average 0.1218, against the plug-in prediction standard error 0.1156 of @eq-mix-prediction-variance-oneway: 5 per cent wider, which is the uncertainty about σa2 that the plug-in throws away, exactly as @prp-mix-bayes(c) says. The same happens for the fixed effect: the posterior standard deviation of μ is 0.0709, against the plug-in λ^1/n=0.0672.

Panel (b) of Figure 32.6.1 repeats the analysis on the first 5 laboratories. The posterior medians are now 0.0435 and 0.0693, a difference of sixty per cent, against a REML estimate of 0.0493. With five groups the prior is doing a large part of the work, and saying so is not optional.

exm-mix-grunfeld.title: Grunfeld’s panel with a random firm effect
exm-mix-grunfeld.title_html: Grunfeld’s panel with a random firm effect
exm-mix-grunfeld.html: Section 6.6 fitted gross investment on market value and capital stock for 11 US firms over 20 years, once with a separate intercept per firm (the within estimator) and once with a single intercept. The mixed model puts the firm effect in between: X holds the intercept, value and capital, Z holds the firm indicators, G=σf2I11 and R=σ2I. Fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (Section 32.4), it gives σ^2=2527.6 and σ^f2=6740.9, a firm standard deviation of 82.1 and an intraclass correlation of 0.727: most of the variation in investment is between firms. The coefficients are 0.1094 for value and 0.3082 for capital, against 0.1101 and 0.3100 for the within estimator and 0.1145 and 0.2275 with a single intercept. The mixed estimate has landed essentially on the within estimate, and Section 32.3 explains why: with 20 years per firm, the weight the model gives to between-firm comparisons is 1−0.9816, less than two per cent.

exm-mix-grunfeld-slopes.title: Do the firms’ slopes differ?
exm-mix-grunfeld-slopes.html:
Continue @exm-mix-grunfeld. Adding a firm-specific slope on market value, with variance σs2 independent of the firm intercept, raises the restricted log-likelihood from −1176.53 to −1159.01. The two models have the same fixed effects, so the comparison is legitimate: the statistic is 35.05 on one boundary parameter, far beyond any reasonable critical value, and AIC falls from 2357.1 to 2324.0, BIC from 2363.8 to 2334.2. The firms’ responses to market value genuinely differ: the estimated standard deviation of the firm-specific slopes is 0.1492.

The consequence for inference is dramatic. In the random-intercept model the coefficient of market value is 0.1094 with standard error 0.0100; in the random-slope model it is 0.0127 with standard error 0.0562, five and a half times larger. Nothing about the data changed. Two things did. The standard error grew because the effective sample size for a population-average slope is 11 firms, not 220 firm-years. The estimate moved because the two models estimate different functionals. Firm-specific intercepts and slopes with a common capital coefficient give eleven slopes of mean −0.0009 and standard deviation 0.198: their spread dwarfs their average. The random-slope model estimates that average; the random-intercept model, forced to give every firm the same slope, reports a precision-weighted blend instead. Panel (a) of Figure 32.5.2 shows the four analyses side by side; panel (b) shows that with 20 years per firm the predicted firm effects are indistinguishable from the firm-indicator estimates.

exm-mix-nested-crossed.title: Nested and crossed random factors
exm-mix-nested-crossed.html: With pupils inside classrooms inside schools, write Z=[Zsch,Zcls] and G=(σS2I00σC2I). Because every classroom belongs to exactly one school, V is block diagonal by school, and the analysis splits school by school; this is the covariance behind @exr-tw-random-classrooms. With subjects responding to items, each subject seeing every item, the two factors are crossed: Zsub and Zitem generate overlapping patterns and V has no block diagonal form at all. Nothing in the theory changes, but the computation does, and crossed random effects are the reason modern software stores Z sparsely.

exm-mix-ols-blue.title: Cluster-constant regressors
exm-mix-ols-blue.html: Take @exm-mix-random-intercept with a balanced layout, nk=m, and suppose every column of X is constant within groups, so that C(X)⊆C(Z). By @eq-mix-balanced-cov, V=λ1M+σ2(I−M) with M the projection onto C(Z), so VX=λ1X and C(VX)=C(X). Ordinary least squares is therefore the best linear unbiased estimator, whatever the variance components are, and the analysis of a balanced cluster-randomized trial can be carried out on the cluster means without loss. The covariance of the estimate is not σ2(X⊤X)−1, however: it is λ1(X⊤X)−1, larger by the factor 1+mγ. Getting the point estimate right and the standard error wrong is the classic error in clustered data.

exm-mix-ols-not-blue.title: Regressors that vary within a cluster
exm-mix-ols-not-blue.title_html: Regressors that vary within a cluster
exm-mix-ols-not-blue.html: Keep the same V, but let X=[1,x] with x varying within groups. Decomposing x into its between and within parts, Vx=λ1Mx+σ2(I−M)x, which lies in C(X) only if one of the two parts vanishes or λ1=σ2. Ordinary least squares is then not efficient, and the reason is visible: generalized least squares downweights the between-group part of x by σ2/λ1=1/(1+mγ) relative to the within-group part, because between-group comparisons carry the extra variance σa2. The mixed estimate is a compromise between the within estimator of Section 6.6, which uses only (I−M)x, and the between estimator, which uses only Mx; as mγ→∞ the weight on the between part goes to zero. @exm-mix-grunfeld is that limit in practice.

exm-mix-proficiency.title: A laboratory proficiency study
exm-mix-proficiency.html:
Twelve laboratories each analyse four aliquots of one homogeneous batch of soil for lead, in mg/kg; the data are simulated so that the truth is known, with μ=2.50, σa=0.20 and σ=0.25, so that the population intraclass correlation is 0.390. The analysis of variance gives MSB=0.2166 on 11 degrees of freedom and MSE=0.0620 on 36, so σ^2=0.0620,σ^a2=0.2166−0.06204=0.0386, that is, a within-laboratory (repeatability) standard deviation of 0.249 and a between-laboratory standard deviation of 0.197. The estimated intraclass correlation is 0.384: about two fifths of the variation in a single measurement is attributable to which laboratory made it.

The F ratio is 3.49, and @eq-mix-gamma-interval gives γ∈(0.118,2.439), that is ρ∈(0.105,0.709). Twelve laboratories and 48 measurements pin the intraclass correlation down only to a factor of seven. That is not a defect of the method; it is what 11 degrees of freedom buy.

exm-mix-random-intercept.title: Random intercepts
exm-mix-random-intercept.html: Observations are grouped, group k contributing nk of them. Take Z to be the n×g matrix of group indicators, G=σa2Ig and R=σ2In, so that V=σ2I+σa2ZZ⊤ as in @prp-mix-oneway(a). The fixed part 𝛃Xβ may hold anything: an intercept alone, recovering @def-mix-oneway; a treatment indicator constant within group, as in a cluster-randomized trial; or regressors that vary within a group, as in a longitudinal study. Each group’s block of V is σ2Ink+σa211⊤, the compound symmetric or equicorrelated form.

exm-mix-random-slope.title: Random intercepts and slopes
exm-mix-random-slope.html: Subject i is measured at times ti1,…,tini, and each subject has its own intercept and its own slope in time: 𝛃Yij=x(ij)⊤β+u0i+u1itij+εij,(u0iu1i)∼N2(0,D), independently across subjects, with 𝛆εi∼Nni(0,σ2I). Here Zi=[1,ti], G=IN⊗D for N subjects, and subject i’s covariance block is Vi=ZiDZi⊤+σ2I, with entries Cov(Yij,Yij′)=d11+d12(tij+tij′)+d22tijtij′+σ21{j=j′}. Two features deserve notice. The variance of a response is quadratic in time, so a random slope model necessarily says that subjects spread apart, or, if d12<0, first converge and then spread. And the correlation between two occasions depends on both times, not only on their separation: it is not stationary. Whether this is the right shape is a modelling question that Chapter 33 takes up.

exm-mix-reml-lab.title: REML and ML for the twelve laboratories
exm-mix-reml-lab.title_html: REML and ML for the twelve laboratories
exm-mix-reml-lab.html:
For the data of @exm-mix-proficiency, @prp-mix-oneway-reml gives σ^2=0.0620 by both methods, and σ^a,REML2=0.0386,σ^a,ML2=0.0341, the maximum likelihood estimate being 0.883 of the restricted one, because it replaces MSB by (g−1)MSB/g before subtracting MSE. The restricted log-likelihood at its maximum is −8.228 and the ordinary log-likelihood is −8.360; the two are not comparable, being likelihoods of 47 and 48 numbers respectively. Both agree with the general matrix formulas coded from @eq-mix-profile and @eq-mix-reml-loglik, and with statsmodels’ MixedLM.

Figure 32.4.1 plots the two profiles against σa2, each with σ2 maximized out: the same shape in different places, the restricted one flatter on the right, which is why REML intervals are wider. Cutting the restricted profile 1.92 units below its maximum gives σa2∈(0.0086,0.1275), an interval comparable to the exact one of @cor-mix-icc-interval and available in models where no exact interval exists.

exm-mix-shrinkage.title: Shrinking twelve laboratories
exm-mix-shrinkage.html:
In @exm-mix-proficiency, σ^2=0.0620 and σ^a2=0.0386 give a shrinkage factor B=0.714. The laboratory deviations y¯k−y¯ run from −0.450 to 0.250; the predicted effects run from −0.321 to 0.178. Each has been pulled about 29 per cent of the way towards zero.

The gain is real. By @eq-mix-prediction-variance-oneway the prediction error variance is 0.01336, a standard error of 0.1156, against 0.01743 for the raw deviation, a ratio of 1.30 in mean squared error. Panel (b) of Figure 32.3.1 shows the comparison over the whole range of intraclass correlations: shrinkage helps most when the correlation is small, which is exactly when the raw deviations are mostly noise.

exr-mix-blup-invariance.title: C1
exr-mix-blup-invariance.html: Show that the BLUP is invariant to reparameterization of the random effects: if Z∗=ZT−1 and G∗=TGT⊤ for a nonsingular T, with u∗=Tu, then V is unchanged and u^∗=Tu^. What does this say about predicting a contrast c⊤u directly versus predicting u and then forming the contrast?

exr-mix-blup-limits.title: A1
exr-mix-blup-limits.html: In @eq-mix-shrinkage, what happens to B as (a) m→∞, (b) σa2→0, (c) σ2→0? Describe in words the predictor in each limit, and say which of the three limits makes the mixed model agree with a fixed-effects analysis.

exr-mix-blup-normal-optimal.title: C2
exr-mix-blup-normal-optimal.html: Assume the normal mixed model and suppose 𝛃β is known. Show that among all predictors t(Y), linear or not, the conditional mean E(c⊤u∣Y) minimizes E(t−c⊤u)2, and that it coincides with the linear predictor of @thm-mix-blup(c). Explain why the same argument does not show that τ^ is optimal among all predictors when 𝛃β is unknown.

exr-mix-blup-of-mean.title: B2
exr-mix-blup-of-mean.html: Take τ=μ+ak, the mean of group k in the balanced one-way model, so that 𝛌λ=1 and c=ek. Use @eq-mix-blup and @eq-mix-prediction-variance to show that the BLUP is y¯+B(y¯k−y¯) with prediction error variance σ2B/m+(1−B)2λ1/n. Show that this equals λ1/n at B=0 and σ2/m at B=1; that it is strictly below σ2/m, the prediction error of the group’s own mean; and that it is below λ1/n as well exactly when mσa2>σ2(g−2), so that it is no interpolation between the two — with g=3, m=4 and σ2=σa2=1 it beats both.

exr-mix-boundary-monotone.title: B2
exr-mix-boundary-monotone.html: Verify directly that the function F↦(n−1)log⁡(aF+b)−(g−1)log⁡F in @eq-mix-ratio-exact vanishes at F=1, is increasing for F>1 and tends to infinity as F→∞. What does the last fact say about the power of the test when σa2 is large?

exr-mix-boundary-two.title: C1
exr-mix-boundary-two.html: Consider testing σa2=0 when a second variance component σb2>0 is present and is not on the boundary. Argue informally that the limiting null distribution is still 12χ2(0)+12χ2(1), and explain why testing both components simultaneously gives a mixture over χ2(0),χ2(1),χ2(2) with weights determined by the probability that the unconstrained maximizer lands in each orthant. Which weights arise if the two estimates are asymptotically independent?

exr-mix-conditional-variance.title: B2
exr-mix-conditional-variance.html: In @prp-mix-bayes(c), suppose 𝛉θ takes only two values with posterior probabilities 1/2 each, giving conditional posterior means u^1,u^2 and common conditional variance v for a coordinate. Compute the correct marginal posterior variance, and say how large the disagreement between u^1 and u^2 must be before the plug-in understates the standard deviation by ten per cent.

exr-mix-crossed-rank.title: C1
exr-mix-crossed-rank.html: Two crossed random factors with a and b levels and one observation per cell give Z=[ZA,ZB] with n=ab, q=a+b. Show that rank(Z)=a+b−1, so Z⊤Z is singular, and explain why this causes no difficulty for @eq-mix-marginal but would if one tried to treat u as a parameter vector to be estimated. Compute V and show it is not block diagonal under any ordering of the observations when a,b≥2.

exr-mix-empirical-bayes-james-stein.title: C2
exr-mix-empirical-bayes-james-stein.html: Take the balanced one-way model with σ2 known, m=1 so that y¯k=yk, and μ known to be zero. Show that plugging the unbiased moment estimate of σa2 into @eq-mix-shrinkage gives a shrinkage factor of the form 1−cσ2/∑kyk2, and compare with the James–Stein estimator of @thm-shr-james-stein. Which constant c does the plug-in give, and which does James–Stein use?

exr-mix-fixed-or-random.title: A1
exr-mix-fixed-or-random.html: For each study, say whether the named factor is better treated as fixed or random, and what the corresponding target of inference is. (a) Four fertilizer formulations compared on a research farm. (b) Twenty operators sampled from a factory’s workforce, each measuring the same set of parts. (c) The two arms of a randomized trial. (d) Thirty schools sampled from a district, in a study of a teaching method. (e) Three furnaces, the only three the plant owns, in a study of their temperature uniformity.

exr-mix-henderson-ridge.title: B3
exr-mix-henderson-ridge.html: Take X empty (no fixed effects), R=σ2I and G=σu2I in @thm-mix-henderson. Show that u^ is exactly the ridge estimate (Z⊤Z+λI)−1Z⊤y with λ=σ2/σu2, and that @eq-mix-prediction-variance becomes σu2c⊤(I+λ−1Z⊤Z)−1c. Compare with the mean squared error of ridge in @thm-shr-ridge: which is the same quantity and which is not?

exr-mix-identifiability.title: A2
exr-mix-identifiability.html: A colleague argues that in @exm-mix-random-intercept the two variance components cannot be separated, since raising σa2 and lowering σ2 both change the diagonal of V in the same direction. Is the argument right? What happens if every group has nk=1?

exr-mix-improper-posterior.title: B1
exr-mix-improper-posterior.html: Show that in the one-way model the marginal posterior density of σa2 under the prior π(σa2)∝σa−2 is not integrable, by showing that exp⁡{ℓR(σa2)} tends to a strictly positive limit as σa2↓0 with σ2 profiled out. Contrast with the behaviour of the prior π(σa)∝1.

exr-mix-kackar-counterexample.title: C2
exr-mix-kackar-counterexample.html: @prp-mix-inference(a) needs the error distribution to be symmetric about zero. Give an example of a translation-invariant, even 𝛉θ^ and a skewed error distribution for which 𝛃𝛉β^(θ^) is biased, and explain why symmetry cannot simply be dropped. (Compare the discussion after @thm-het-wls.)

exr-mix-m0.title: B1
exr-mix-m0.html: Verify @eq-mix-m0 directly from the group means: show that E{∑knk(Y¯k−Y¯)2}=σ2(g−1)+σa2(n−∑knk2/n) by computing Var(Y¯k), Var(Y¯) and Cov(Y¯k,Y¯). Confirm that m0=m when the layout is balanced, and that m0≤(n−minknk)/(g−1) in general.

exr-mix-negative-probability.title: B3
exr-mix-negative-probability.html: Using @eq-mix-negative, compute Pr(σ^a2<0) when σa2=0, for (g,m)=(5,4) and (g,m)=(25,4). Explain why the probability does not tend to 0 as g→∞ with σa2=0 fixed, and why it does tend to 0 for any fixed σa2>0.

exr-mix-ols-blue-blocks.title: B2
exr-mix-ols-blue-blocks.html: Let V=λ1M+σ2(I−M) as in @eq-mix-balanced-cov. Show that C(VX)⊆C(X) holds if and only if C(X) decomposes as (C(X)∩C(Z))⊕(C(X)∩C(Z)⊥), that is, iff M maps C(X) into itself. Give an X with both between and within columns for which ordinary least squares is best.

exr-mix-prior-is-random-effect.title: A1
exr-mix-prior-is-random-effect.html: Explain in two sentences why a random effect and a prior are formally the same object, and name one thing that distinguishes them in practice.

exr-mix-raw-mse.title: B1
exr-mix-raw-mse.html: Show that the predictor Y¯k−Y¯ of ak in the balanced one-way model has E(Y¯k−Y¯−ak)2=σ2(1−1/g)/m+σa2/g, and verify that @eq-mix-prediction-variance-oneway is smaller for every γ>0. Where does the difference come from when γ is very small?

exr-mix-reml-bayes-preview.title: C1
exr-mix-reml-bayes-preview.html: Show that 𝛃𝛉𝛃𝛉∫exp⁡{ℓ(β,θ)}dβ=exp⁡{ℓR(θ)} when rank(X)=p and the constant 12log⁡det(X⊤X) is dropped from @eq-mix-reml-loglik. (Hint: complete the square in 𝛃β and use the normal integral.) This identity is the subject of Section 32.6; state in words what it says about REML.

exr-mix-reml-contrasts.title: B1
exr-mix-reml-contrasts.html: Verify @thm-mix-reml(b) directly in the simplest case: n=3, X=13, V=diag(v1,v2,v3). Choose a basis K of 1⊥, compute K(K⊤VK)−1K⊤ and P, and check they agree. Then change K to a different basis and confirm that det(K⊤VK) changes by a factor free of V.

exr-mix-reml-lrt-fixed.title: A2
exr-mix-reml-lrt-fixed.html: A colleague tests whether a regressor belongs in the fixed part of a mixed model by comparing restricted log-likelihoods with and without it, referring twice the difference to χ2(1). Give two separate reasons why this is wrong, and say what to do instead.

exr-mix-reml-ordinary.title: A1
exr-mix-reml-ordinary.html: Take V=σ2I and rank(X)=p. Show from @eq-mix-reml-vs-ml that −2ℓR=(n−p)log⁡σ2+SSE/σ2 up to constants, and deduce that the REML estimate of σ2 is s2. Then use @prp-opt-divisor to find which multiple of SSE has the smallest mean squared error, and show that the maximum likelihood estimator beats s2 for some (n,p) and loses to it for others.

exr-mix-reml-prior.title: C1
exr-mix-reml-prior.html: Formula @eq-mix-marginal-posterior shows REML is the posterior mode of 𝛉θ under a flat prior on 𝛉θ. A mode is not invariant to reparameterization: the mode of the posterior of σa2 is not the square of the mode of the posterior of σa. Reconcile this with @thm-mix-reml(c), which says the REML estimate is well defined. What is invariant, and what is not?

exr-mix-reml-scale.title: A2
exr-mix-reml-scale.html: A colleague reports two restricted log-likelihoods for the same model fitted to the same data, differing by 6.91, the only difference between the runs being that one measured a regressor in units and the other in thousands. Explain the discrepancy using @eq-mix-reml-vs-ml, and confirm the value 6.91.

exr-mix-reml-score-check.title: B3
exr-mix-reml-score-check.html: Specialize the score equations @eq-mix-scores of @prp-mix-scores to the balanced one-way model with 𝛉θ=(λ1,λ2), for which V=λ1M+λ2(I−M), V1=M and V2=I−M. Show that the restricted score equations are λ^1=MSB and λ^2=MSE, recovering @prp-mix-oneway-reml(a) without any optimization.

exr-mix-reml-two-groups.title: B2
exr-mix-reml-two-groups.html: Two groups of sizes n1,n2 have independent normal responses with a common mean and variances σ2 and cσ2 with c known. Write down ℓP and ℓR for σ2, find both maximizers, and confirm that REML divides by n1+n2−1 and ML by n1+n2.

exr-mix-satterthwaite-exact.title: B1
exr-mix-satterthwaite-exact.html: Apply @eq-mix-satterthwaite to the estimated variance 4MSC/(gm) of @prp-mix-inference(b), a single multiple of one mean square, and confirm that it returns ν=g−2 exactly. Then apply it to σ^a2=(MSB−MSE)/m in the balanced one-way model and write down the resulting degrees of freedom.

exr-mix-truncation.title: C1
exr-mix-truncation.html: Let T be any estimator of σa2≥0 and T+=max(T,0). Show that E(T+−σa2)2≤E(T−σa2)2, with strict inequality whenever Pr(T<0)>0. Deduce that the truncated moment estimator dominates the unbiased one in mean squared error, and explain why this does not make the unbiased estimator useless.

exr-mix-two-way-random.title: C2
exr-mix-two-way-random.html: Consider a balanced two-way layout with a levels of A, b levels of B, m observations per cell, and all effects random: Yijk=μ+αi+βj+(αβ)ij+εijk with the four sets uncorrelated and variances σA2,σB2,σAB2,σ2. Using the Kronecker projections of Section 16.3 and @thm-rv-quadform-mean, show that EMSA=σ2+mσAB2+bmσA2,EMSAB=σ2+mσAB2. Which ratio tests σA2=0? Contrast this with the fixed-effects analysis, where MSA/MSE is the right ratio.

exr-mix-variance-of-estimate.title: B2
exr-mix-variance-of-estimate.html: In the balanced normal model, use @prp-mix-oneway(d) to show that Var(σ^a2)=2m2{(σ2+mσa2)2g−1+σ4n−g}. With σ2 and σa2 fixed and n=gm held constant, is the variance smaller with many small groups or few large ones?

exr-mix-vinverse-oneway.title: B1
exr-mix-vinverse-oneway.html: Specialize @eq-mix-v-inverse to @exm-mix-random-intercept with group sizes nk, and show that the kth block of V−1 is 1σ2(Ink−σa2σ2+nkσa211⊤). Deduce that the generalized least squares criterion is σ−2∑k{∑jrkj2−wknkr¯k2} with wk=nkσa2/(σ2+nkσa2), and interpret wk.

exr-mix-wald-variance-component.title: B3
exr-mix-wald-variance-component.html: In the balanced one-way model, compute the Wald interval σ^a2±1.96se for the proficiency study using @exr-mix-variance-of-estimate for the standard error with the estimates plugged in, and compare it with the exact interval implied by @cor-mix-icc-interval and with the profile interval (0.0086,0.1275) of @exm-mix-reml-lab. Comment.

exr-mix-why-t.title: A1
exr-mix-why-t.html: In @prp-mix-inference(b), the reported standard error is exactly right and the test is still wrong. Explain in one or two sentences what “exactly right” means here and what is wrong, and say why the problem gets worse as the intraclass correlation grows with n fixed.

exr-mix-write-down-v.title: A1
exr-mix-write-down-v.html: A study measures 3 subjects on 2 occasions each, with a random subject effect of variance σs2 and independent errors of variance σ2. Write Z, G, R and V explicitly as 6×6 or 6×3 matrices, and check @eq-mix-v-inverse numerically for σs2=2, σ2=1.

lem-mix-P.title: The residual operator P
lem-mix-P.html:
Let V be positive definite and r=rank(X). The matrix P of @eq-mix-P does not depend on the choice of generalized inverse, and

  1. PX=0, PVP=P, P is symmetric and rank(P)=n−r;

  2. 𝛃Py=V−1(y−Xβ^) and y⊤Py=minb(y−Xb)⊤V−1(y−Xb);

  3. if V depends smoothly on 𝛉θ and Vj=∂V/∂θj, then ∂P/∂θj=−PVjP.

prp-mix-bayes.title: BLUP as a posterior mean, REML as a marginal posterior
prp-mix-bayes.title_html: BLUP as a posterior mean, REML as a marginal posterior
prp-mix-bayes.html:
Consider @eq-mix-hierarchy with G and R positive definite and rank(X)=p.

  1. (BLUP is a posterior mean.) Fix 𝛉θ and take the improper flat prior 𝛃π(β)∝1. Then the joint posterior of 𝛃(β,u) is 𝛃𝛃(βu)|y∼Np+q((β^u^), C−1), with 𝛃β^,u^ and C as in @thm-mix-henderson. In particular E(u∣y)=u^ is the BLUP, 𝛃𝛃E(β∣y)=β^ is the generalized least squares estimate, and Cov(u∣y) is the prediction error covariance of @eq-mix-prediction-variance.

  2. (REML is a marginal posterior.) With the flat prior on 𝛃β and any prior 𝛉π(θ), the marginal posterior of the variance components is 𝛉𝛉𝛉π(θ∣y) ∝ π(θ)exp⁡{ℓR(θ)},{#eq-mix-marginal-posterior}

    with ℓR the restricted log-likelihood of @def-mix-reml. The REML estimate is therefore the mode of the marginal posterior under a flat prior on 𝛉θ.

  3. (What the plug-in leaves out.) Under (a) with 𝛉θ replaced by an estimate, the reported posterior variance is 𝛉Cov(u∣y,θ^), whereas the correct marginal posterior variance is 𝛉𝛉E{Cov(u∣y,θ)∣y}+Cov{E(u∣y,θ)∣y}. The plug-in omits the second term, so it is too small.

prp-mix-inference.title: Fixed-effect inference with an estimated covariance
prp-mix-inference.title_html: Fixed-effect inference with an estimated covariance
prp-mix-inference.html:
Consider the normal linear mixed model with rank(X)=p, and write 𝛃𝛉β^(θ)=(X⊤V−1X)−1X⊤V−1Y for the generalized least squares estimator.

  1. (Unbiasedness.) Let 𝛉𝛉θ^=θ^(Y) be translation invariant, meaning 𝛉𝛉θ^(y+Xb)=θ^(y) for all b, and even, meaning 𝛉𝛉θ^(−y)=θ^(y). If 𝛃𝛉E‖β^(θ^)‖<∞, then 𝛃𝛉𝛃Eβ^(θ^)=β. Both REML and maximum likelihood estimators of 𝛉θ have these two properties.

  2. (A design where everything is exact.) Consider a balanced cluster-randomized trial: g clusters, g/2 assigned to each arm, m units per cluster, with a random cluster effect of variance σa2 and independent errors of variance σ2. Let β^ be the difference of the two arms’ means of cluster means, and let MSC be the mean square between clusters within arms, on g−2 degrees of freedom, and MSE the mean square within clusters. Then, with λ1=σ2+mσa2, Var(β^)=4λ1/(gm) and β^−β4MSC/(gm)∼t(g−2){#eq-mix-cluster-t}

    exactly. If MSC≥MSE then MSC is also the REML estimate of λ1; otherwise the REML estimate lies on the boundary σ^a2=0, as in @prp-mix-oneway-reml(c).

  3. (Satterthwaite’s approximation.) Let U=∑iciMSi>0, where the MSi are independent and νiMSi/EMSi∼χ2(νi). The two-moment match of Section 4.3, fitting νU/EU∼χ2(ν) to the mean and variance of U, has ν=(EU)2∑ici2(EMSi)2/νi,{#eq-mix-satterthwaite}

    estimated in practice by replacing EMSi by MSi.

The companion statement for the variance components themselves, where the null value sits on the boundary of the parameter space, is @thm-mix-boundary below.

prp-mix-oneway.title: The one-way random effects model
prp-mix-oneway.html:
In @def-mix-oneway, write γ=σa2/σ2 and let M be the projection onto C(Z), which replaces each entry by its group mean.

  1. E(Y)=μ1 and Cov(Y)=σ2I+σa2ZZ⊤, a block diagonal matrix whose kth block is σ2Ink+σa211⊤.

  2. (Intraclass correlation.) Observations in different groups are uncorrelated, and two observations in the same group have correlation ρ=σa2σa2+σ2=γ1+γ∈[0,1).

  3. (Moment estimates.) Let MSB and MSE be the between and within mean squares of the one-way analysis of variance, on g−1 and n−g degrees of freedom. Then E(MSE)=σ2 and E(MSB)=σ2+m0σa2 with m0=1g−1(n−∑knk2n),{#eq-mix-m0}

    which equals m in a balanced layout. Hence σ^2=MSE and σ^a2=(MSB−MSE)/m0 are unbiased.

  4. (Distributions, balanced and normal.) If the layout is balanced and the model is normal, then with λ1=σ2+mσa2, SSBλ1∼χ2(g−1)independently ofSSEσ2∼χ2(n−g), and therefore MSB/MSE∼(1+mγ)F(g−1,n−g).

prp-mix-oneway-reml.title: Balanced one-way: ML and REML
prp-mix-oneway-reml.html:
In the balanced normal one-way random effects model, write λ1=σ2+mσa2 and λ2=σ2, and treat (λ1,λ2) with λ1≥λ2>0 as the parameters. Then, up to constants free of the parameters, −2ℓP=glog⁡λ1+(n−g)log⁡λ2+SSBλ1+SSEλ2,{#eq-mix-oneway-ml}

−2ℓR=(g−1)log⁡λ1+(n−g)log⁡λ2+SSBλ1+SSEλ2.{#eq-mix-oneway-reml}

The two criteria differ in one coefficient, but leave the interior of the parameter space at different moments.

  1. When MSB≥MSE, REML gives λ^1=MSB, λ^2=MSE, so σ^2=MSE and σ^a2=(MSB−MSE)/m: the moment estimates of @prp-mix-oneway(c), which are unbiased.

  2. When MSB≥gMSE/(g−1), maximum likelihood gives λ^1=SSB/g, λ^2=MSE, so σ^ML2=MSE and σ^a,ML2=1m(g−1gMSB−MSE).

    The right-hand side is the unconstrained maximizer whatever the data, it is nonnegative exactly under the stated condition, and E{1m(g−1gMSB−MSE)}−σa2=−λ1gm.{#eq-mix-ml-bias}

  3. Otherwise the maximizer lies on the boundary λ1=λ2 and the method returns σ^a2=0 with σ^2 the pooled mean square: for REML when MSB<MSE, for maximum likelihood on the wider range MSB<gMSE/(g−1). Between the two thresholds the REML estimate of σa2 is positive and the ML estimate is zero.

prp-mix-scores.title: Score equations
prp-mix-scores.html:
Let Vj=∂V/∂θj and P be as in @eq-mix-P. Then ∂ℓP∂θj=−12{tr(V−1Vj)−y⊤PVjPy},∂ℓR∂θj=−12{tr(PVj)−y⊤PVjPy},{#eq-mix-scores}

The restricted score exceeds the profile score by 12tr{(X⊤V−1X)−X⊤V−1VjV−1X}, which is nonnegative whenever Vj is nonnegative definite, as it is for a variance-component parameterization V=∑jθjZjZj⊤.

prp-mix-vinverse.title: The inverse and determinant of V
prp-mix-vinverse.title_html: The inverse and determinant of V
prp-mix-vinverse.html:
Let R and G be positive definite in @def-mix-model. Then V is positive definite, and V−1=R−1−R−1Z(G−1+Z⊤R−1Z)−1Z⊤R−1,{#eq-mix-v-inverse}

detV=detRdetGdet(G−1+Z⊤R−1Z).{#eq-mix-v-determinant}

If in addition the observations fall into g clusters with R=⨁kRk, Z=⨁kZk and G=⨁kGk block diagonal, the last saying that different clusters’ random effects are independent, then V=⨁k(ZkGkZk⊤+Rk) is block diagonal too, and everything decomposes cluster by cluster.

thm-mix-blup.title: Best linear unbiased prediction
thm-mix-blup.html:
In @def-mix-model let V=ZGZ⊤+R be positive definite and let 𝛌λ∈C(X⊤). Put 𝛃𝛃β^=(X⊤V−1X)−X⊤V−1Y,u^=GZ⊤V−1(Y−Xβ^).{#eq-mix-blup}

  1. The BLUP of 𝛌𝛃τ=λ⊤β+c⊤u is 𝛌𝛃τ^=λ⊤β^+c⊤u^. It does not depend on which generalized inverse is used, and it is the unique minimizer.

  2. Its prediction error variance is E(τ^−τ)2=c⊤(G−GZ⊤V−1ZG)c+d⊤(X⊤V−1X)−d,{#eq-mix-prediction-variance}

    where 𝛌d=λ−X⊤V−1ZGc.

  3. If 𝛃β were known, the best linear predictor of τ would be 𝛌𝛃𝛃λ⊤β+c⊤GZ⊤V−1(Y−Xβ), with prediction error variance the first term of @eq-mix-prediction-variance. The second term is the price of estimating 𝛃β.

thm-mix-boundary.title: Exact null distribution of the restricted likelihood ratio
thm-mix-boundary.title_html: Exact null distribution of the restricted likelihood ratio
thm-mix-boundary.html:
In the balanced normal one-way random effects model with n=gm, let L=2{supσa2≥0ℓR−supσa2=0ℓR} be the restricted likelihood ratio statistic for H0:σa2=0, and write F=MSB/MSE, a=(g−1)/(n−1), b=(n−g)/(n−1). Then L={0,F≤1,(n−1)log⁡(aF+b)−(g−1)log⁡F,F>1.{#eq-mix-ratio-exact}

Under H0, F∼F(g−1,n−g), so the null distribution of L is free of σ2 and exactly computable. In particular L is a nondecreasing function of F and Pr(L=0)=Pr{F(g−1,n−g)≤1}, a probability that tends to 12 as g and n−g grow.

thm-mix-henderson.title: Henderson’s mixed model equations
thm-mix-henderson.html:
Let G and R be positive definite and rank(X)=p. Define C=(X⊤R−1XX⊤R−1ZZ⊤R−1XZ⊤R−1Z+G−1),h=(X⊤R−1yZ⊤R−1y).{#eq-mix-henderson}

  1. C is positive definite, and the unique solution of C(b⊤,v⊤)⊤=h is 𝛃b=β^, the generalized least squares estimate, and v=u^, the BLUP of @eq-mix-blup.

  2. The same pair is the unique minimizer of the penalized least squares criterion 𝛃𝛃𝛃Q(β,u)=(y−Xβ−Zu)⊤R−1(y−Xβ−Zu)+u⊤G−1u.{#eq-mix-penalized}

  3. With W=X⊤V−1X, the blocks of C−1 are (C−1)11=W−1,(C−1)12=−W−1X⊤V−1ZG, (C−1)22=G−GZ⊤V−1ZG+GZ⊤V−1XW−1X⊤V−1ZG. Its leading block is 𝛃Cov(β^) and its trailing block is Cov(u^−u), the matrix whose quadratic forms are @eq-mix-prediction-variance.

thm-mix-reml.title: The restricted likelihood
thm-mix-reml.html:
In @def-mix-reml, with V positive definite:

  1. K⊤Y∼Nn−r(0,K⊤VK) with K⊤VK positive definite, so @eq-mix-reml-loglik is its log-likelihood.

  2. K(K⊤VK)−1K⊤=P for every admissible K. In particular the quadratic form in @eq-mix-reml-loglik equals y⊤Py and does not depend on K.

  3. Two admissible K1,K2 give restricted log-likelihoods differing by a constant free of 𝛉θ. Hence the REML estimate does not depend on which maximal set of error contrasts is used.

  4. If rank(X)=p, then for any admissible K with K⊤K=I, det(K⊤VK)=detVdet(X⊤V−1X)det(X⊤X),{#eq-mix-reml-determinant}

    so that 𝛉𝛉ℓR(θ)=ℓP(θ)+p2log⁡2π−12log⁡det(X⊤V−1X)+12log⁡det(X⊤X).{#eq-mix-reml-vs-ml}
